Einstein ring explorer

A massive galaxy bends the light of a galaxy far behind it into arcs, or a ring. The ring's size weighs the lens. Pick a lens, then drag the background galaxy around in the right-hand panel and set the lens's mass and shape with the sliders. The middle panel shows what that lens would do; the left panel is what Hubble actually saw.

What Hubble saw

F814W image minus our model of the lens galaxy's light. Dashed: your lens model's critical curve (white) and the published one (violet).

What your lens predicts

The background galaxy, seen through the lens (same scale, 6.4″ across).

Behind the lens: the source plane

Drag the galaxy (or use arrow keys). Solid: caustic; dashed: cut. Crossing them adds images.

Data: Hubble ACS/WFC F814W images (MAST Hubble Advanced Products) of the SLACS lenses; redshifts and velocity dispersions from Bolton et al. (2008) and Auger et al. (2009). Lens models: singular isothermal ellipsoid + Sérsic source, fitted in this project. The match score compares the predicted image (scaled to its best brightness) with the data inside the fitted region; it ignores the telescope's blurring beyond a small smoothing, so 100% is out of reach. Distances assume H0 = 70 km/s/Mpc, Ωm = 0.3.
